steps: The thermal stability of hydrogen halides decreases down the group.
The chlorine atom is smaller than the bromine atom, so the H—Cl bond is stronger than the H—Br bond.
The weaker H—Br bond breaks more readily on heating; therefore, hydrogen bromide is thermally less stable than hydrogen chloride.
items.finalAnswer: Hydrogen bromide is less thermally stable because its H—Br bond is weaker than the H—Cl bond in hydrogen chloride.

steps: Metals are generally solids at room temperature; non-metals may be solids, liquids or gases.
Metals are generally lustrous, whereas non-metals are generally dull.
Metals are malleable and ductile; solid non-metals are generally brittle.
Metals are generally good conductors of heat and electricity; non-metals are generally poor conductors.
Metals are generally sonorous; non-metals are non-sonorous.
Metals generally form positive ions by losing electrons; non-metals generally form negative ions by gaining electrons.
Metal oxides are generally basic, whereas non-metal oxides are generally acidic.
items.finalAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous, malleable, ductile, sonorous, good conductors and form positive ions; non-metals generally show the opposite properties and form negative ions.

steps: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) is less expensive than platinum.
Platinum is easily poisoned by impurities present in the reacting gases, which reduces its catalytic activity.
V₂O₅ is not poisoned as readily and is an effective catalyst for the oxidation of sulphur dioxide.
items.finalAnswer: V₂O₅ is preferred because it is cheaper than platinum and is less readily poisoned by impurities.

steps: Liquid sodium is circulated through the reactor core, where it absorbs heat produced during nuclear reactions.
The hot sodium carries this heat to a heat exchanger, where it is transferred to water to produce steam.
The steam is used to drive a turbine and generate electricity.
Sodium is used because it is an excellent conductor of heat.
items.finalAnswer: Sodium transfers heat from the reactor core to water in a heat exchanger; its high thermal conductivity is utilized.

steps: Lithium behaves differently from the other alkali metals because its atom and ion are exceptionally small.
The small size gives lithium ion a high charge density and strong polarizing power; lithium also has comparatively high ionization energy.
Consequently, lithium is harder and has higher melting and boiling points than the other alkali metals, and it reacts less vigorously with water.
Lithium forms the normal oxide Li₂O and combines directly with nitrogen to form lithium nitride, Li₃N.
items.finalAnswer: Lithium shows anomalous behaviour because its very small size gives it high charge density and polarizing power.

steps: Aluminium is a good conductor of heat, so it is suitable for cooking utensils.
It is light and malleable, so it can be made into utensils easily.
A thin, protective layer of aluminium oxide forms on its surface and prevents further corrosion.
Magnesium is more reactive and can burn in air; therefore, it is not considered suitable for cooking utensils.
items.finalAnswer: Aluminium is used for cooking utensils because it conducts heat well and resists corrosion, while the more reactive magnesium may burn in air.
